q: In Mendel's crosses, the offspring produced by crossing two pure-breeding parent plants with contrasting traits form the:
x: The two pure-breeding parents are the P generation and their offspring are the F1. The F2 is obtained only when the F1 plants are self-pollinated.

q: An organism carrying two identical alleles of a gene, such as TT or tt, is described as:
x: Homozygous means both alleles of a gene are the same (TT or tt). A heterozygote or hybrid carries two different alleles (Tt); hemizygous means only one copy is present, as with X-linked genes in males.

q: Mendel referred to the hereditary units that control characters as:
x: Mendel called them 'factors'. The word 'gene' was introduced later (by Johannsen, 1909), and chromosomes were not linked to heredity in Mendel's time.

q: Mendel's work was rediscovered in 1900 by:
x: In 1900 Carl Correns, Hugo de Vries and Erich von Tschermak independently rediscovered Mendel's laws. Morgan and his students later worked on Drosophila linkage.

q: A dominant allele is one that:
o: Is expressed only when two copies are present
Is always more common in a population
Expresses its effect even in the heterozygous condition
Always mutates into the recessive allele
x: A dominant allele shows its effect in the heterozygote (Tt looks like TT). Needing two copies to be expressed describes a recessive allele; dominance says nothing about how common an allele is.

q: Mendel's law of dominance states that:
o: When two contrasting alleles are present together, only one of them is expressed in the phenotype
The two alleles of a gene separate when gametes are formed
Alleles of different genes enter gametes independently of each other
Genes on the same chromosome are inherited together
x: The law of dominance says that in a hybrid only one of the two contrasting factors (the dominant one) shows. Separation of alleles is the law of segregation, and independent entry of different genes is the law of independent assortment.

q: The term 'genotype' means:
o: The visible form of a character
The set of alleles an organism carries for a character
The number of chromosomes in a gamete
The effect of the environment on a trait
x: Genotype is the genetic make-up, for example TT, Tt or tt. The visible form of the character (tall or dwarf) is the phenotype.

q: Contrasting forms of one character, such as round and wrinkled seed shape, are called:
x: A character (seed shape) has contrasting traits (round, wrinkled). A locus is a gene's position, a genome is the full set of genes, and a linkage group is the genes on one chromosome.

q: In his F2 for seed shape, Mendel counted 5474 round and 1850 wrinkled seeds. These numbers are closest to the ratio:
x: 5474 ÷ 1850 is about 2.96, which is very close to 3 : 1, the monohybrid F2 phenotypic ratio. 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotypic ratio, not the phenotypic one.

q: A pure axial-flowered pea plant is crossed with a pure terminal-flowered plant. Axial is dominant. The F1 plants have:
o: Axial and terminal flowers in a 3 : 1 ratio
x: The F1 of two pure lines is all heterozygous, and with complete dominance it shows only the dominant trait, axial flowers. A 3 : 1 ratio appears only in the F2.

q: In the F2 of a monohybrid cross (Tt × Tt), the ratio of homozygous plants to heterozygous plants is:
x: The F2 is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Homozygous plants (TT + tt) are 2 out of 4 and heterozygous (Tt) are 2 out of 4, giving 1 : 1.

q: All the tall plants of a monohybrid F2 (from Tt × Tt) are self-pollinated, each giving equal numbers of offspring. What fraction of the resulting F3 plants is expected to be dwarf?
x: Of the tall F2 plants, 1/3 are TT (no dwarf offspring) and 2/3 are Tt (1/4 dwarf offspring). Dwarf fraction = 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/6.

q: Which pair of parents can produce offspring that are half round-seeded and half wrinkled-seeded? (Round, R, is dominant.)
x: Rr × rr gives 1 Rr : 1 rr, that is half round and half wrinkled. Two heterozygotes give 3 : 1, and any cross with a homozygous round parent gives only round offspring.

q: Two heterozygous pea plants (Rr × Rr) produce 600 seeds. About how many seeds are expected to be heterozygous (Rr)?
x: Rr × Rr gives 1/4 RR, 1/2 Rr and 1/4 rr. Half of 600 is 300. 450 would be the number of round seeds (3/4), not heterozygous ones.

q: In four o'clock plants, flower colour shows incomplete dominance. A pink-flowered plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant. The offspring are expected to be:
x: Pink is RW and white is WW. RW × WW gives 1 RW (pink) : 1 WW (white). The 1 : 2 : 1 ratio comes only from pink × pink.

q: In a monohybrid cross showing incomplete dominance, the F2 phenotypic ratio and genotypic ratio are:
o: Both 1 : 2 : 1, because each genotype has its own phenotype
x: With incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, so each of the three genotypes looks different and both ratios are 1 : 2 : 1. Under complete dominance the phenotypic ratio would be 3 : 1.

q: The ABO blood group is controlled by three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i). How many different genotypes are possible?
x: The genotypes are IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi, IᴬIᴮ and ii, which is 6. Four is the number of blood group phenotypes (A, B, AB, O).

q: A man with blood group A (Iᴬi) marries a woman with blood group B (Iᴮi). Their children can have blood groups:
o: Any of the four groups: A, B, AB or O
Groups A, B and AB, but never O
x: Iᴬi × Iᴮi gives IᴬIᴮ (group AB), Iᴬi (group A), Iᴮi (group B) and ii (group O), each with probability 1/4. Because both parents carry i, a group O child is possible.

q: A child has blood group O and the mother has blood group A. Which blood group is NOT possible for the father?
x: A group O child is ii, so the father must pass on an i allele. A group AB father (IᴬIᴮ) has no i allele. A father of group A can be Iᴬi, a father of group B can be Iᴮi, and a group O father is ii.

q: For an autosomal recessive condition, a couple are both heterozygous (Aa). What is the chance that their first child is unaffected and their second child is affected?
x: Each birth is independent. P(unaffected) = 3/4 and P(affected) = 1/4, so the chance of this order is 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16.

q: Tall (T) is completely dominant over dwarf (t). Which cross gives a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio among the offspring?
x: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, which is 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Tt × tt gives 1 : 1, and any cross with a TT parent gives only tall offspring.

q: A pea plant of genotype Tt forms gametes. In what proportion are they produced?
o: Three quarters carry T and one quarter carry t
All carry both T and t
Half carry T and half carry t
x: By the law of segregation the two alleles separate at meiosis, so each gamete gets one allele and T and t gametes form in equal numbers. No gamete carries both.

q: The phenotype of an organism is the result of:
o: Its genotype alone, unaffected by its surroundings
Its genotype acting together with the environment
The number of its chromosomes only
x: Genes set the potential, and the environment influences how it is expressed, so phenotype = genotype + environment. Neither the genotype alone nor the environment alone fully decides it.

q: Mendel removed the anthers from the flowers of one parent plant before they matured. The purpose was to:
o: Prevent self-pollination so that the cross could be controlled
Increase the number of seeds produced
x: Pea flowers normally self-pollinate. Removing the immature anthers (emasculation) stopped this, so Mendel could dust pollen from the chosen male parent and control the cross.

q: Reciprocal crosses in peas (tall female × dwarf male, and dwarf female × tall male) gave identical F1 results. This showed that:
o: The tall allele is carried only by the male
The dwarf allele is lost during fertilisation
It did not matter which parent, male or female, contributed each allele
Height in peas is controlled by the environment
x: Identical results from reciprocal crosses show that both parents contribute equally and the trait does not depend on the sex of the parent. The dwarf allele is not lost; it reappears in the F2.

q: The F1 of a monohybrid cross (Tt) is self-pollinated. What fraction of the F2 plants will breed true when they are themselves self-pollinated?
x: Only homozygous plants breed true. In the F2, TT (1/4) and tt (1/4) together make 1/2. The Tt plants (1/2) segregate again.

q: Which of the following was a key reason for the success of Mendel's experiments?
o: He could see genes on chromosomes under the microscope
He studied one or two characters at a time and analysed large numbers of offspring mathematically
He worked on Drosophila, which breeds quickly
He chose characters whose genes were linked on one chromosome
x: Mendel followed a few clear contrasting characters, used pure lines, counted large numbers and analysed the ratios. Genes and chromosomes were unknown to him, Drosophila was Morgan's organism, and linked genes would have hidden independent assortment.

q: A cross in which the parents differ in two pairs of contrasting characters is called a:
x: A dihybrid cross follows two characters at once, such as seed shape and seed colour. A monohybrid cross follows only one character.

q: Mendel crossed pure-breeding RRYY peas with pure-breeding rryy peas. What is true of the genotype of each F1 hybrid?
o: It carries two dominant alleles of each gene (RRYY)
It carries two recessive alleles of each gene (rryy)
It carries one dominant and one recessive allele of each gene (RrYy)
It is heterozygous for seed shape only (RrYY)
x: The RRYY parent gives only RY gametes and the rryy parent only ry gametes, so every F1 plant is RrYy, with round yellow seeds.

q: In Mendel's classic example of independent assortment in peas, the two characters followed together were:
x: Mendel's well-known dihybrid cross was round yellow × wrinkled green seeds, so the characters were seed shape and seed colour.

q: A pea plant RrYy produces gametes in which proportions?
o: Only RY and ry, in equal proportions
RY and ry more often than Ry and rY
RY, Ry, rY and ry in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio
RY, Ry, rY and ry in equal proportions (1 : 1 : 1 : 1)
x: Because the two genes assort independently, each allele of one gene combines equally often with each allele of the other, giving four gamete types in equal numbers. 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 is the F2 phenotype ratio, not a gamete ratio.

q: An individual of genotype AaBbCC forms gametes, with the genes assorting independently. Which statement is correct?
o: Half of the gametes carry the c allele
Every gamete carries the C allele
It forms eight types of gametes
No gamete carries the A allele together with the b allele
x: The individual is homozygous CC, so every gamete gets C. Only the two heterozygous genes vary, giving 2 × 2 = 4 gamete types, and the combination of A with b is one of them.

q: In the cross AaBbCc × aabbcc, with independent genes and complete dominance, what fraction of the offspring shows the dominant phenotype for all three traits?
x: For each gene, Aa × aa gives 1/2 dominant offspring. For all three: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. 27/64 would be the answer for AaBbCc × AaBbCc.

q: In the cross AaBb × aaBb, with the genes assorting independently, what fraction of the offspring is expected to be aabb?
x: Aa × aa gives aa with probability 1/2, and Bb × Bb gives bb with probability 1/4. Multiplying, 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

q: Two individuals heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb) are crossed. The chance that an offspring is heterozygous for the first gene but homozygous recessive for the second is:
x: P(Aa) from Aa × Aa is 1/2 and P(bb) from Bb × Bb is 1/4. Since the genes assort independently, 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

q: In a trihybrid cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc with three independent genes, how many different genotypes can occur among the offspring?
x: Each gene gives three genotypes (for example AA, Aa, aa), so three independent genes give 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 different genotypes. 64 is the number of gamete combinations (Punnett boxes) and 8 the number of gamete types per parent.

q: With complete dominance for each gene, how many phenotypic classes are expected in the offspring of AaBbCc × AaBbCc?
x: Each gene gives two phenotypes (dominant or recessive), so three genes give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 classes. 27 is the number of genotypes.

q: An individual is heterozygous for n genes that assort independently. The number of different gametes it can form is:
x: Each heterozygous gene gives two choices of allele, and the choices are independent, so the gamete types are 2 × 2 × ... = 2ⁿ. For example AaBb (n = 2) gives 4 gametes. 3ⁿ counts genotypes in the offspring of two such parents.

q: Which individual produces only one type of gamete?
o: One heterozygous for a single gene
One homozygous for all of its genes
x: Gamete variety comes from heterozygous genes, each giving two possible alleles. An individual homozygous for every gene (for example AABBcc) can make only one kind of gamete.

q: In the cross AaBb × AaBb, what fraction of the offspring shows the recessive phenotype for gene A but the dominant phenotype for gene B?
x: P(aa) = 1/4 and P(B_) = 3/4, so P(aaB_) = 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16. This is one of the two 3/16 classes of the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.

q: The independent assortment of different homologous chromosome pairs takes place during:
o: Metaphase I and anaphase I of meiosis
x: Each homologous pair lines up at metaphase I with a random orientation, and the pairs separate at anaphase I. That is when alleles of genes on different chromosomes are sorted independently.

q: Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can independent assortment produce in human gametes (n = 23)?
x: Each of the 23 pairs can orient in two ways, independently of the others, so the number of combinations is 2²³, about 8.4 million. This is a major source of variation.

q: A true-breeding round green line of peas is crossed with a true-breeding wrinkled yellow line. The hybrid seeds will be:
o: Round green and wrinkled yellow in equal numbers
x: RRyy × rrYY gives only RrYy. Round and yellow are dominant, so all hybrid seeds are round yellow, a combination that neither parent showed.

q: A and B are completely dominant and unlinked. Which cross gives offspring in a 1 : 1 phenotypic ratio?
o: Heterozygous for one gene, homozygous dominant for the other × double recessive
x: AaBB × aabb gives AaBb and aaBb in equal numbers: all show B and half show A, so 1 : 1. AaBb × aabb gives 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, AABB × aabb gives one class, and AaBb × AaBb gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

q: In a dihybrid F2 (RrYy selfed), the round yellow class is made up of how many distinct genotypes?
x: Round yellow plants can be RRYY, RRYy, RrYY or RrYy, which is four genotypes. Nine is the total number of genotypes in the whole F2.

q: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb), what fraction of the offspring is homozygous for one gene and heterozygous for the other?
x: For each gene, P(homozygous) = 1/2 and P(heterozygous) = 1/2. Homozygous A with heterozygous B is 1/4, and heterozygous A with homozygous B is another 1/4, so the total is 1/2.

q: What is the probability that a gamete from an AaBbCc individual, with independent genes, carries A, B and C together?
x: Each gene puts its dominant allele into a gamete with probability 1/2, independently, so the chance is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8.

q: Round green and wrinkled yellow seeds appeared in Mendel's dihybrid F2, although the original parents were round yellow and wrinkled green. This shows that:
o: The genes for seed shape and seed colour are sorted into gametes independently
Round and yellow are always inherited together
Mutations arose in the F1 plants
Seed colour depends on seed shape
x: New combinations appear because the alleles for shape and for colour separate independently at gamete formation. If round always went with yellow, these new types could not arise.

q: Looking at seed colour alone among the plants of a dihybrid F2 (RrYy selfed), the genotypes YY, Yy and yy occur in the ratio:
x: Each gene in a dihybrid cross still follows the monohybrid pattern, so Yy × Yy gives 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy. The 3 : 1 is the phenotypic ratio for colour.

q: A dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy yields 640 seeds. The expected number of rryy seeds is:
x: P(rryy) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, and 640 ÷ 16 = 40. 120 would be each 3/16 class and 360 the 9/16 class.

q: In the cross AaBbCcDd × AaBbCcDd, with independent genes, what fraction of the offspring is homozygous dominant for all four genes?
x: For each gene, P(homozygous dominant) = 1/4. For four genes: (1/4)⁴ = 1/256.

q: In a dihybrid F2 (AaBb × AaBb), what fraction of the offspring shows the dominant phenotype for gene A, whatever its phenotype for gene B?
x: Because gene B assorts independently, it does not affect the result for gene A: Aa × Aa gives 3/4 A_. 9/16 is the fraction dominant for both genes.

q: The law of independent assortment describes the inheritance of:
o: The two alleles of a single gene
Genes located close together on one chromosome
Two or more different characters controlled by different genes
Characters controlled only by the environment
x: Independent assortment is about how genes for different characters are sorted relative to each other. The separation of the two alleles of one gene is the law of segregation, and closely placed genes on one chromosome are linked.

q: In Mendel's dihybrid experiment, which seed colour was dominant?
x: Yellow seed colour is dominant over green in peas, which is why all F1 seeds of round yellow × wrinkled green were yellow. Green reappeared only in the F2.

q: Genes located on the same chromosome are said to be:
x: Genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together. Alleles are forms of one gene at one locus, and genes on different chromosomes assort independently.

q: All the genes carried on one chromosome together form a:
x: The genes of one chromosome make up a linkage group. A genome is the whole set of genes, a gene pool is all the genes of a population, and a karyotype is the chromosome set as seen in a picture.

q: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes results in:
x: Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids gives new combinations of alleles, called recombination. It does not change the chromosome number.

q: The garden pea has 2n = 14. How many linkage groups does it have?
x: The number of linkage groups equals the haploid number. With 2n = 14, n = 7, so peas have 7 linkage groups.

q: In male Drosophila, crossing over normally does not occur. As a result, linked genes in males show:
x: Without crossing over, linked genes are never separated, which is complete linkage. Incomplete linkage needs occasional crossing over, as in female Drosophila.

q: Two genes lie very close together on the same chromosome. They will be:
o: Separated by crossing over in every meiosis
x: The chance of a crossover between two loci depends on the distance between them, so very close genes are seldom separated and are strongly linked.

q: During crossing over, the broken segments of non-sister chromatids are joined again by the enzyme:
x: In crossing over the chromatids break (by endonuclease) and the exchanged pieces are sealed by DNA ligase. Helicase unwinds DNA and polymerases build new strands.

q: In the human body, which cells normally carry out crossing over?
o: Cells of the gonads undergoing meiosis to form gametes
x: Crossing over happens in prophase I of meiosis, which occurs in the testes and ovaries when gametes are made. Body cells divide by mitosis, where it does not normally occur.

q: The protein framework that holds homologous chromosomes closely paired during synapsis is the:
x: The synaptonemal complex forms between homologues during synapsis and keeps them tightly paired so crossing over can occur. The spindle moves chromosomes later in division.

q: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes that must happen before crossing over, begins in which substage of prophase I?
x: Homologues begin pairing in zygotene; crossing over follows in pachytene. In leptotene the chromosomes are only starting to condense, and in diplotene they begin to separate at the chiasmata.

q: Chiasmata move towards the ends of the chromosomes (terminalisation). This is completed in which substage of prophase I?
x: Terminalisation of chiasmata is completed in diakinesis, the last substage of prophase I. Chiasmata become visible in diplotene, after crossing over in pachytene.

q: Crossing over takes place at the four-strand stage. This means it occurs:
o: Before DNA replication, when each homologue is a single strand
After DNA replication, when each homologue has two chromatids
After the homologues have separated in anaphase I
During the S phase of interphase
x: DNA is replicated in interphase, so in prophase I each bivalent has four chromatids. Crossing over takes place then, between two of these four, and before anaphase I.

q: Which statement about gene linkage is NOT correct?
o: Linked genes always assort independently of each other
Linked genes lie on the same chromosome
Linked genes tend to be inherited together
Linkage can be broken by crossing over
x: Linked genes lie on one chromosome and tend to stay together, which is why they do not assort independently. Crossing over can separate them.

q: Genes X, Y and Z lie on one chromosome. Map distances are X–Y 20 units, Y–Z 15 units and X–Z 5 units. Which gene lies in the middle?
o: The order cannot be worked out from these data
x: The largest distance (X–Y, 20) must be between the two outer genes. X–Z (5) + Z–Y (15) = 20, so the order is X–Z–Y and Z is in the middle.

q: In a dihybrid whose two linked genes are in the repulsion (trans) arrangement, the homologous chromosomes carry:
o: One dominant and one recessive allele each (Ab and aB)
AB on one homologue and ab on the other
The two genes on two different chromosome pairs
x: In repulsion each homologue has one dominant and one recessive allele (Ab/aB). AB on one homologue and ab on the other is the coupling (cis) arrangement.

q: In a bivalent of an AB/ab dihybrid, a crossover occurs, but outside the region between loci A and B. For these two genes, the chromatids will carry:
o: Two parental and two recombinant combinations
New alleles created by the crossover
x: Only a crossover between two loci separates their alleles. A crossover outside that region keeps the dominant alleles together on one chromatid and the recessive alleles together on the other, so all chromatids stay parental for these genes.

q: Crossing over alters which of the following?
o: The number of chromosomes in each gamete
The combination of alleles carried on a chromatid
x: Crossing over swaps corresponding segments between homologues, so it reshuffles alleles on chromatids. The number of chromosomes and the ploidy are unchanged.

q: Two human genes lie on chromosome 3 and chromosome 11 respectively. These two genes:
x: Linkage applies only to genes on the same chromosome. Genes on different chromosomes belong to different linkage groups and assort independently.

q: The segments exchanged between non-sister chromatids during crossing over are:
o: Corresponding segments carrying alleles of the same genes
Random segments of any length from any chromosome
Segments from sister chromatids of the same chromosome
Whole arms swapped with non-homologous chromosomes
x: Crossing over is a reciprocal exchange of equivalent segments between homologous non-sister chromatids, so alleles of the same genes change places. Exchange with non-homologous chromosomes would be a translocation.

q: Map units (centimorgans) on a linkage map measure:
o: The exact physical length of DNA in nanometres
The number of genes between two loci
Relative distance worked out from recombination frequency
The time taken for crossing over
x: A map unit equals 1% recombination. It gives the relative distance between genes based on how often they are separated by crossing over, not a physical length.

q: Gene X is 12 map units from gene Y, and gene Y is 7 map units from gene Z. Ignoring double crossovers, the distance between X and Z could be:
x: Z may lie on the far side of Y from X (12 + 7 = 19) or between X and Y (12 − 7 = 5). Without the X–Z value, both orders are possible.

q: A recombination frequency of 0% between two genes shows that they are:
o: Separated by crossing over in every meiosis
x: No recombinants means crossing over never separated the genes, which is complete linkage. Unlinked genes or genes on different chromosomes give 50% recombination.

q: Incomplete linkage means that linked genes:
o: Are usually inherited together but are occasionally separated by crossing over
x: In incomplete linkage, crossing over sometimes separates the linked genes, giving a few recombinants. Genes that are never separated show complete linkage.

q: Chiasmata hold the homologous chromosomes of a bivalent together until they separate at:
x: Homologues stay joined at chiasmata through metaphase I and separate at anaphase I. Anaphase II separates sister chromatids, not homologues.

q: After crossing over, a chromatid that carries a mix of maternal and paternal alleles is called a:
x: A chromatid that took part in the exchange has a new combination of alleles and is recombinant. The chromatids not involved keep the parental combination.

q: When crossing over does occur between two linked loci in a coupling heterozygote (AB/ab), the total number of gamete types it can produce becomes:
x: Without crossing over only AB and ab form. Crossing over between the loci adds the recombinants Ab and aB, making four types, though the parental types remain more frequent.

q: Mendel's law of independent assortment holds fully for two genes that are located:
o: Close together on the same chromosome
x: Genes on different (non-homologous) chromosomes are shuffled independently at metaphase I. Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and tend to stay together.

q: Without crossing over, a coupling dihybrid (AB/ab) makes two kinds of gametes. With crossing over between the genes, it can make:
x: Crossing over adds the two recombinant gametes, Ab and aB, to the parental AB and ab, giving four kinds in all.

q: Linkage between two genes is said to be complete when:
o: Crossing over occurs in every meiotic cell
The two genes lie on different chromosomes
Recombinants make up exactly half of the offspring
No crossing over occurs between them, so only parental types appear
x: In complete linkage the genes are never separated, so the dihybrid gives only parental combinations. Recombinants at 50% would mean the genes behave as unlinked.

q: A test cross uses a dihybrid in repulsion, Ab/aB, whose genes recombine with a frequency of 20%. Offspring showing both dominant traits should make up:
x: In repulsion, AB is a recombinant gamete. Recombinants total 20%, split equally between AB and ab, so AB gametes and hence AaBb offspring are 10%.

q: A plant has the repulsion arrangement Ab/aB of two genes that never cross over, with complete dominance. On selfing, its progeny phenotypes appear in the ratio:
x: Only Ab and aB gametes form, giving Ab/Ab, Ab/aB and aB/aB in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio. These show the phenotypes A_bb, A_B_ and aaB_; no aabb appears.

q: From the results of a test cross, how can you tell whether a linked dihybrid had its genes in coupling or in repulsion?
o: From the total number of offspring
From whether all four classes appear
From the phenotype of the recessive tester
From which two offspring classes are the most frequent
x: The most frequent classes are the parental types, showing the allele combinations on the parent's chromosomes. AaBb and aabb most common means coupling; Aabb and aaBb means repulsion.

q: Compared with two genes that assort independently, two tightly linked genes:
o: Increase the number of recombinant offspring
Give the four test-cross classes in equal numbers
Are separated in every meiotic division
Reduce the variety of allele combinations among the offspring
x: Tightly linked genes rarely separate, so most offspring repeat the parental combinations and fewer new combinations appear.

q: A dihybrid is produced by crossing AAbb with aaBB, and the two genes are linked. In its test cross, which offspring will be the rare recombinants?
o: AaBb (both dominant traits) and aabb (both recessive)
Aabb (trait A only) and aaBb (trait B only)
AaBb and Aabb (all showing trait A)
aaBb and aabb (all lacking trait A)
x: The dihybrid received Ab from one parent and aB from the other, so it is in repulsion. Its new combinations are AB and ab, giving AaBb and aabb offspring.

q: Two genes lie on the same chromosome, yet a dihybrid test cross gives a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio. The best explanation is that:
o: Crossing over does not occur on that chromosome
They are so far apart that a crossover between them occurs in nearly every meiosis
x: Very distant genes on one chromosome recombine about 50% of the time, so they give the same ratio as unlinked genes.

q: Genes A, B and C lie close together on one chromosome and are completely linked (ABC/abc). How many kinds of gametes form, compared with the number if the genes were on different chromosomes?
x: With complete linkage only the parental chromosomes ABC and abc go into gametes. Three independently assorting genes would give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 kinds.

q: Crossing over between genes A and B produces new allele combinations only when the individual is:
x: If either locus is homozygous, exchanging segments swaps identical alleles and nothing new forms. Both loci must be heterozygous for recombinants to arise.

q: Why are recombinant offspring of linked genes fewer than the parental types?
o: A crossover between the two genes occurs in only some meiotic cells
Crossing over occurs only in males
x: In most meiotic cells no crossover happens between the two loci, and even a crossover affects only two of the four chromatids. So parental gametes stay in the majority.

q: The recombination frequency is 8% between genes P and Q, and 3% between Q and R. The recombination frequency between P and R could be:
x: If R lies between P and Q, P–R is 8 − 3 = 5%. If Q lies between P and R, P–R is 8 + 3 = 11%. A third distance is needed to decide.

q: Which cross is used to find out whether genes A and B are linked?
o: A cross between two double homozygous dominants
A test cross of the dihybrid with a double recessive
A cross of the dihybrid with a double homozygous dominant
A cross between two double recessives
x: Crossing AaBb with aabb shows the gametes of the dihybrid directly. Equal classes mean independent assortment; excess parental classes mean linkage.

q: Crossing over in a coupling dihybrid (AB/ab) always produces Ab and aB gametes in about equal numbers because:
o: Ab gametes are always more viable than aB
Crossing over occurs between sister chromatids
Each crossover is a reciprocal exchange between two chromatids
x: In a crossover two non-sister chromatids swap segments, so each event gives one Ab and one aB chromatid.

q: In a test cross of a linked dihybrid with aabb, the percentage of recombinant offspring equals the percentage of:
o: Recombinant gametes formed by the aabb parent
Recombinant gametes formed by the dihybrid parent
Meiotic cells with a chiasma anywhere
Parental gametes formed by the dihybrid
x: The aabb parent gives only ab gametes, so each offspring shows the gamete of the dihybrid. Recombinant offspring therefore reflect its recombinant gametes.

q: Recombination frequencies are 12% between genes X and Y, 7% between Y and Z, and 5% between X and Z. Which gene lies in the middle?
o: The order cannot be worked out
x: The largest distance (X–Y, 12) is between the two outer genes, and 5 + 7 = 12. So the order is X–Z–Y, with Z in the middle.

q: Genes A and B are 30 map units apart. A dihybrid with the arrangement Ab/aB is expected to form what percentage of AB gametes?
x: With repulsion (Ab/aB), AB and ab are the recombinant gametes. Total recombinants are 30%, shared equally, so AB = 15%. Ab and aB are 35% each.

q: Crossing over does not normally occur in male Drosophila. A grey long male (BV/bv) is crossed with a black vestigial female. The offspring will be:
o: Mostly parental types with a few recombinants
Grey long and black vestigial only, 1 : 1
x: Without crossing over, the male forms only BV and bv gametes, so only the two parental phenotypes appear in equal numbers. This is complete linkage.

q: Two genes give an F2 ratio very close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. This shows that the two genes are:
o: Two alleles of the same gene
x: A 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio is the result of independent assortment. Linked genes give an excess of parental types instead.

q: The chromosome set of a normal human female body cell is:
x: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes: 44 autosomes and two sex chromosomes, XX in females. 22 + X is the set in an egg.

q: The X and Y chromosomes, which differ between the sexes, are also called:
x: Sex chromosomes are also called allosomes or heterosomes. Autosomes are the chromosomes that are the same in both sexes.

q: Genes on the part of the Y chromosome that has no matching part on the X are called:
x: Genes found only on the Y are holandric (Y-linked) and are passed only from father to son. X-linked genes are on the X chromosome.

q: In Drosophila, as in humans, the heterogametic sex is:
x: Drosophila uses the XX–XY system: females are XX and males XY. XO is found in grasshopper males and ZW in female birds.

q: In birds, which use the ZW system, a male bird has the sex chromosomes:
x: In birds the male is homogametic (ZZ) and the female heterogametic (ZW), the reverse of humans.

q: In birds, the sex of a chick is decided by:
o: The type of sperm produced by the father
The temperature at which the egg is kept
The number of autosomes in the egg
The type of egg produced by the mother
x: The hen (ZW) makes Z-bearing and W-bearing eggs, while the cock (ZZ) makes only Z sperm. So the egg decides the sex, unlike in humans.

q: In an insect with the XX–XO system, the male has 23 chromosomes in his body cells. His sperm will carry:
x: The male has 22 autosomes + one X. Each sperm gets 11 autosomes, and half also get the X (12) while half get no sex chromosome (11).

q: A person has 44 autosomes and a single X chromosome (XO). This person develops as:
x: Without a Y chromosome the body develops as female (Turner's syndrome, usually sterile). This shows that the Y, not the number of X chromosomes, causes maleness.

q: The human Y chromosome decides maleness because it carries a gene that causes the embryo to develop:
x: A gene on the Y (the testis-determining factor) makes the embryonic gonads develop into testes. Without it, ovaries form.

q: A normal human sperm contains how many chromosomes in all?
x: A sperm is haploid: 22 autosomes plus one sex chromosome (X or Y), 23 in total.

q: A boy has an X-linked allele. Which of these relatives could NOT have passed this allele to him?
x: A boy's only X comes from his mother, who got it from either of her parents. His father gave him a Y, so nothing X-linked can reach him from the father's side.

q: Which of the following is NOT true of the human Y chromosome?
o: It is smaller than the X chromosome
It is passed from a father to his sons
It carries the gene for red–green colour vision
It is present only in males
x: The colour-vision genes lie on the X chromosome, which is why colour blindness is X-linked. The other statements about the Y are true.

q: How many sex chromosomes are present in a normal human body cell?
x: Each body cell has one pair of sex chromosomes: XX in females and XY in males. The other 44 are autosomes.

q: For three children of the same parents, what is the probability that at least one will be a son?
x: The chance that all three are daughters is 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. So the chance of at least one son is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

q: In which of these groups is the female the heterogametic sex?
x: In birds the female is ZW and makes two kinds of eggs. In mammals and Drosophila the male is XY, and in grasshoppers the male is XO.

q: For an X-linked recessive allele to show its effect in a woman, she must be:
o: Carrying the allele on her Y chromosome
x: A woman has two X chromosomes, so the recessive allele shows only when both X chromosomes carry it. A heterozygous woman is a carrier with normal phenotype.

q: Which cells of a normal human male contain an X chromosome but no Y chromosome?
x: Body cells and primary spermatocytes are XY. When the sex chromosomes separate in meiosis, half the sperm receive the X and half the Y.

q: A human egg is fertilised by a sperm carrying 22 + Y. The zygote will be:
x: The egg always gives 22 + X. Adding 22 + Y gives 44 + XY, which develops as a male.

q: A woman is heterozygous for an X-linked allele. What fraction of her sons are expected to receive this allele?
x: Each son gets one of her two X chromosomes at random, so on average half receive the allele. Sons get nothing X-linked from the father.

q: Which statement correctly compares autosomes and sex chromosomes in humans?
o: Autosomes differ between males and females
Sex chromosomes carry only genes for sex
Autosomes are found only in body cells, not in gametes
Autosomes are alike in both sexes, while the sex chromosome pair differs
x: The 22 pairs of autosomes are the same in males and females; only the sex chromosome pair differs (XX or XY). The X also carries many genes not linked to sex, and gametes contain autosomes too.

q: If Xᶜ stands for the colour-blindness allele, a colour-blind man has the genotype:
x: A man has one X and one Y; the gene is on the X only. So a colour-blind man is XᶜY. The Y carries no allele for this gene.

q: When the father is colour-blind and the mother heterozygous, the expected fraction of colour-blind children, sons and daughters together, is:
x: XᶜY × XᶜX gives XᶜXᶜ, XᶜX, XᶜY and XY in equal numbers. Two of the four (a daughter and a son) are colour-blind, which is 1/2.

q: A colour-blind father and a carrier mother have daughters. These daughters are expected to be:
o: Half carriers and half homozygous normal
x: Every daughter gets the father's Xᶜ. From the mother she gets Xᶜ or a normal X with equal chance, so half are colour-blind and half are carriers.

q: A colour-blind woman and a man with normal vision have a daughter. This daughter marries a man with normal vision. What is the probability that a son of hers is colour-blind?
x: The daughter got Xᶜ from her mother and a normal X from her father, so she is certainly a carrier. Each of her sons has a 1/2 chance of receiving Xᶜ.

q: In a family tree, which observation would rule out X-linked recessive inheritance of a trait?
o: An affected man has unaffected parents
An affected man has only unaffected sons
Two unaffected parents have an affected son
An affected woman has a son with the normal phenotype
x: An affected woman has the allele on both X chromosomes, so every son must receive it and be affected. A normal son of hers rules out X-linked recessive inheritance.

q: If Xʷ is the white-eye allele, a white-eyed male Drosophila has the genotype:
x: The white-eye gene is on the X chromosome and absent from the Y, so a white-eyed male carries one Xʷ with a Y.

q: A heterozygous red-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a red-eyed male. The offspring are expected to be:
o: All daughters red-eyed; half the sons white-eyed
Half the daughters and half the sons white-eyed
All sons white-eyed; all daughters red-eyed
x: Every daughter gets the father's red X, so all are red-eyed. Sons get one of the mother's two X chromosomes, so half are white-eyed.

q: A white-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a white-eyed male. The offspring are expected to be:
o: All white-eyed, both males and females
x: Both parents carry only the white allele (XʷXʷ and XʷY), so every offspring receives Xʷ and no red allele. All are white-eyed.

q: From the cross XᵂXʷ × XʷY in Drosophila, the fraction of white-eyed flies expected among all the progeny is:
x: XᵂXʷ × XʷY gives XᵂXʷ, XʷXʷ, XᵂY and XʷY in equal numbers. White-eyed females and white-eyed males together make 1/2.

q: Drosophila is suitable for genetic studies for all of the following reasons EXCEPT that it:
o: Has a very large number of chromosomes
Has a short life cycle of about two weeks
Produces many offspring from each cross
Is small and easy to culture in the laboratory
x: Drosophila has only four pairs of chromosomes, which makes its genetics easier to follow. Its short life cycle, many offspring and easy culture are real advantages.

q: Which observation shows that the white-eye gene of Drosophila is NOT on the Y chromosome?
o: The first white-eyed fly Morgan found was a male
White-eyed males can have white-eyed offspring
Male flies carry only one X chromosome
x: Females have no Y chromosome, so a Y-linked trait could never appear in them. White-eyed females therefore show the gene is not on the Y but on the X. A white-eyed male, or a male passing the trait on, would fit Y-linkage too.

q: Hairy ear rims are inherited as a holandric trait. Which grandchildren of an affected man will certainly inherit it from him?
o: All the sons of his daughters
All the children of his daughters
All the sons of his sons
All the daughters of his sons
x: A Y-linked gene passes from father to every son, and then on to every son of those sons. Daughters receive no Y, so the trait cannot pass through them.

q: The allele for red–green colour blindness is called recessive because:
o: It is found only in males
A carrier woman with one copy has normal colour vision
It is carried on the Y chromosome
It appears in every generation of a family
x: A heterozygous woman sees colours normally: the normal allele masks the colour-blindness allele. That is what makes it recessive.

q: A girl is red–green colour-blind. From whom did she receive the colour-blindness alleles?
o: One from her father and one from her mother
One from her mother and one from a grandparent directly
x: She needs the allele on both X chromosomes, and she received one X from each parent. So her father is colour-blind and her mother at least a carrier.

q: Which of the following human disorders is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait?
x: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, like hemophilia and colour blindness, is X-linked recessive. Albinism and phenylketonuria are autosomal recessive, and hairy ear rims are Y-linked.

q: Two parents with normal vision have a colour-blind son and a daughter with normal vision. The daughter marries a man with normal vision. What is the probability that her first child is a colour-blind son?
x: The mother must be a carrier, so the daughter has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier. If she is, the chance of a colour-blind son is 1/4. So 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.

q: Y-linked (holandric) traits never appear in females because females:
o: Have two X chromosomes that mask them
Carry only recessive alleles of these genes
x: Holandric genes are found only on the Y chromosome. Females are XX, so they cannot carry or show these traits.

q: An X-linked recessive trait often seems to skip a generation because it is passed on through:
o: Carrier daughters who do not show the trait
Sons who carry it on their Y chromosome
Affected fathers to all their sons
x: An affected man's daughters are carriers with normal phenotype; the trait then reappears in about half of their sons.

q: Whether a son is colour-blind depends only on:
o: The genotypes of both parents equally
The genotype of his paternal grandfather
x: A son receives his only X from his mother and a Y from his father. So his colour vision is decided by the X he gets from her.

q: A red-eyed female Drosophila crossed with a red-eyed male gives 120 offspring, of which 30 are white-eyed males. Which conclusion is correct?
o: The female is heterozygous, and no white-eyed females are expected
The female is homozygous red, and some white-eyed females are expected
The male carries the white allele on his Y
Both parents are heterozygous, so a quarter of the females are white-eyed
x: White-eyed sons must get Xʷ from the mother, so she is XᵂXʷ. Every daughter gets the father's red X, so none are white-eyed.

q: Because it appeared in several European ruling families, hemophilia is often called:
x: Hemophilia spread through many European royal families from Queen Victoria, who was a carrier, so it became known as the royal disease.

q: If Xʰ is the hemophilia allele, a man with hemophilia has the genotype:
x: The hemophilia gene is on the X only, so an affected man has one Xʰ and a Y. XᴴY is a normal man.

q: A woman who is a carrier for hemophilia usually has normal blood clotting because:
o: Her one normal allele makes enough of the clotting factor
Her Y chromosome carries a normal allele
The hemophilia allele is not expressed in females
x: A carrier is XᴴXʰ. The normal allele on one X produces enough clotting factor, so the recessive allele is masked.

q: In a family the father has hemophilia and the mother is heterozygous. What is the chance that any son of theirs is affected?
x: A son's X comes only from his mother, who has one Xʰ and one Xᴴ. So each son has a 1/2 chance; the father's allele does not reach sons.

q: A woman with hemophilia (XʰXʰ) marries a normal man. Their children are expected to be:
o: All sons hemophilic and all daughters carriers
Half the sons hemophilic and all daughters normal non-carriers
All sons normal and all daughters hemophilic
x: Every child gets an Xʰ from the mother. Sons have no other X and are hemophilic; daughters also get the father's Xᴴ and are carriers.

q: The daughter of a hemophilic man clots normally, and her husband is normal. Before birth, when the sex is unknown, the chance that their baby is hemophilic is:
x: She received Xʰ from her father, so she is a carrier. A child has a 1/2 chance of being a son and a 1/2 chance of getting Xʰ: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

q: Which test result is typical of a person with hemophilia?
o: A very low red blood cell count
x: In hemophilia a clotting factor is missing, so blood takes much longer to clot. The platelet count is usually normal.

q: The most common form of hemophilia is:
o: Hemophilia B, due to lack of factor IX
Hemophilia A, due to lack of factor VIII
Hemophilia B, due to lack of factor VIII
Hemophilia A, due to lack of platelets
x: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) makes up most cases. Hemophilia B, or Christmas disease, is due to factor IX deficiency and is less common.

q: In severe hemophilia, repeated internal bleeding commonly occurs into the:
x: Bleeding into joints (and muscles) is a typical feature of severe hemophilia and can damage the joints over time.

q: Two sons are born to an XᴴXʰ mother and an XᴴY father. The chance that only one of the two boys is hemophilic is:
x: Each son has a 1/2 chance of being affected. Exactly one affected can happen two ways (first or second son): 2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/2.

q: Which person can NOT pass the hemophilia allele to any of his or her children?
o: A woman whose father had hemophilia
x: A man with normal clotting is XᴴY and has no Xʰ to pass on. A woman with normal clotting could still be a carrier.

q: A woman with normal clotting has a hemophilic father. Her genotype must be:
x: Her father could give her only his Xʰ. Since her clotting is normal, her other X carries Xᴴ, so she is a carrier.

q: An XᴴY father and an XᴴXʰ mother have a first son who is hemophilic. The chance that the next baby is a girl who clots normally is:
x: Every daughter gets the father's Xᴴ, so all daughters clot normally. The chance of a daughter is 1/2, and the earlier son does not change this.

q: A student lists four facts about hemophilia. Which one is NOT correct?
o: Affected females are much rarer than affected males
Its allele is carried on the Y chromosome
It is caused by a recessive allele
A carrier woman passes the allele to about half her children
x: The hemophilia allele is on the X chromosome, not the Y. The other statements are true of an X-linked recessive disorder.

q: In hemophilia, the part of blood that is deficient is:
o: A clotting factor protein in plasma
x: Hemophilia is a lack of a plasma clotting factor, such as factor VIII. Platelets, red cells and white cells are normal.

q: Which of these crosses can produce a daughter with hemophilia?
x: A hemophilic daughter needs Xʰ from both parents, so the father must be XʰY and the mother must carry Xʰ. Only XᴴXʰ × XʰY fits.

q: An XᴴXʰ mother and an XᴴY father have a daughter. She later marries a man with hemophilia. The chance that her first baby is hemophilic is:
x: The daughter has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier. If she is, with a hemophilic husband half of all her children are affected: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

q: A hemophilic man and a carrier woman have a son with hemophilia. From whom did the son inherit the hemophilia allele?
o: Both his father and his mother
Neither; it is a new mutation in the son
x: A son receives his X only from his mother; the father gives him a Y. So even with a hemophilic father, the son's allele came from his carrier mother.

q: The hemophilia allele of an affected man most often shows up again in his:
x: He passes Xʰ to all his daughters, who are carriers, and they pass it to about half their sons. His sons get his Y, not the allele.
